### References

- [1] The onset of symptoms in myocardial infarction (MI) is usually gradual, over several minutes, and rarely instantaneous. Chest pain is the most common symptom of acute MI and is often described as a sensation of tightness, pressure, or squeezing. Chest pain due to ischemia (a lack of blood and hence oxygen supply) of the heart muscle is termed angina pectoris. Pain radiates most often to the left arm, but may also radiate to the lower jaw, neck, right arm, back, and upper abdomen, where it may mimic heartburn. Levine's sign, in which a person localizes the chest pain by clenching their fists over their sternum, has classically been thought to be predictive of cardiac chest pain, although a prospective observational study showed it had a poor positive predictive value.

#1910
Q: What are parapodia?
Gold: unjointed paired extensions of the body wall
Answer: Parapodia are unjointed paired extensions of the body wall found in polychaetes, a class of segmented worms. These extensions function as limbs and are often supported internally by one or more large, thick chetae. In burrowing and tube-dwelling polychaetes, parapodia are typically just ridges whose tips bear hooked chetae. In more active forms, such as crawlers and swimmers, parapodia are often divided into large upper and lower paddles on a very short trunk. These paddles are generally fringed with chetae and sometimes with cirri (fused bundles of cilia) and gills, aiding in locomotion and respiration.

### References

- [1] Polychaetes: A Class of Segmented Worms That Produce Trochophore Larvae
- [2] Parapodia: Unjointed Paired Extensions of the Body Wall in Polychaetes

#1911
Q: Why did most scientists accept the validity of evolution by the 1870s, but considered natural selection a minor part of it?
Gold: they believed evolution was purposeful and progressive.
Answer: By the mid-1870s, most scientists had accepted the concept of evolution, but they relegated natural selection to a minor role. They believed that evolution was purposeful and progressive, and this view influenced their understanding of the mechanisms driving evolutionary change. The range of evolutionary theories during this period included various forms of "saltationism," which proposed that new species arose through sudden, large changes rather than gradual adaptation. Orthogenesis, another theory, suggested that species had an inherent tendency to change in a particular direction. Neo-Lamarckism, which proposed that acquired characteristics could be inherited, leading to progress, was also a prevalent view. The minority view of August Weismann, that natural selection was the only mechanism, was called neo-Darwinism. However, the rediscovery of Mendelian inheritance was thought to invalidate Darwin's views, leading to a diminished role for natural selection in the scientific community.

### References

- [1] By the mid-1870s, most scientists accepted evolution, but relegated natural selection to a minor role as they believed evolution was purposeful and progressive. The range of evolutionary theories during "the eclipse of Darwinism" included forms of "saltationism" in which new species were thought to arise through "jumps" rather than gradual adaptation, forms of orthogenesis claiming that species had an inherent tendency to change in a particular direction, and forms of neo-Lamarckism in which inheritance of acquired characteristics led to progress. The minority view of August Weismann, that natural selection was the only mechanism, was called neo-Darwinism. It was thought that the rediscovery of Mendelian inheritance invalidated Darwin's views.

#1923
Q: Where did the Gothic architecture style originate?
Gold: France
Answer: Gothic architecture originated in 12th-century France. It evolved from Romanesque architecture and was characterized by the use of ribbed vaults, pointed arches, and flying buttresses. This architectural style was used primarily in the construction of cathedrals and churches, and it continued to be used until the 16th century in much of Europe.

### References

- [1] Gothic architecture is a style of architecture that flourished during the high and late medieval period. It evolved from Romanesque architecture and was succeeded by Renaissance architecture. Originating in 12th-century France and lasting into the 16th century, Gothic architecture was known during the period as Opus Francigenum (\"French work\") with the term Gothic first appearing during the later part of the Renaissance. Its characteristics include the pointed arch, the ribbed vault and the flying buttress. Gothic architecture is most familiar as the architecture of many of the great cathedrals, abbeys and churches of Europe. It is also the architecture of many castles, palaces, town halls, guild halls, universities and to a less prominent extent, private dwellings, such as dorms and rooms.
- [2] From the early 12th century, French builders developed the Gothic style, marked by the use of rib vaults, pointed arches, flying buttresses, and large stained glass windows. It was used mainly in churches and cathedrals, and continued in use until the 16th century in much of Europe. Classic examples of Gothic architecture include Chartres Cathedral and Reims Cathedral in France as well as Salisbury Cathedral in England. Stained glass became a crucial element in the design of churches, which continued to use extensive wall-paintings, now almost all lost.

Gold: mathematical astronomy

His work in this area was influenced by his belief that the stars are self-luminous and that the planets, including Venus, are also self-luminous. He used his observations, such as the transit of Venus, to help establish the position of Venus in Ptolemaic cosmology, which was a geocentric model of the universe prevalent at the time.

### References

- [1] Avicenna's astronomical writings had some influence on later writers, although in general his work could be considered less developed than Alhazen or Al-Biruni. One important feature of his writing is that he considers mathematical astronomy as a separate discipline to astrology. He criticized Aristotle's view of the stars receiving their light from the Sun, stating that the stars are self-luminous, and believed that the planets are also self-luminous. He claimed to have observed Venus as a spot on the Sun. This is possible, as there was a transit on May 24, 1032, but Avicenna did not give the date of his observation, and modern scholars have questioned whether he could have observed the transit from his location at that time; he may have mistaken a sunspot for Venus. He used his transit observation to help establish that Venus was, at least sometimes, below the Sun in Ptolemaic cosmology, i.e. the sphere of Venus comes before the sphere of the Sun when moving out from the Earth in the prevailing geocentric model.

#1953
Q: Was child labour common in European colonies?
Gold: child labour was common place in the colonies of European
Answer: Child labour was indeed common in the European colonies, particularly during the colonial period between 1650 and 1950. Colonial administrators encouraged traditional kin-ordered modes of production, which included hiring entire households, not just adults, for work. Millions of children were employed in various industries such as agricultural plantations, mines, and domestic service. For instance, the Masters and Servants Act of 1899, passed by Britain, was used to encourage child labour in its colonies, particularly in Africa. Additionally, sophisticated schemes like Pauper Apprenticeship were implemented, where children as young as 5 to 14 years old were hired as apprentices without pay, often away from their parents, to learn a craft. These practices were widespread and supported by colonial governments to meet their economic needs.

### References

- [1] Systematic use of child labour was common place in the colonies of European powers between 1650 and 1950. In Africa, colonial administrators encouraged traditional kin-ordered modes of production, that is hiring a household for work not just the adults. Millions of children worked in colonial agricultural plantations, mines and domestic service industries. Sophisticated schemes were promulgated where children in these colonies between the ages of 5–14 were hired as an apprentice without pay in exchange for learning a craft. A system of Pauper Apprenticeship came into practice in the 19th century where the colonial master neither needed the native parents' nor child's approval to assign a child to labour, away from parents, at a distant farm owned by a different colonial master. Other schemes included 'earn-and-learn' programs where children would work and thereby learn. Britain for example passed a law, the so-called Masters and Servants Act of 1899, followed by Tax and Pass Law, to encourage child labour in colonies particularly in Africa. These laws offered the native people the legal ownership to some of the native land in exchange for making labour of wife and children available to colonial government's needs such as in farms and as picannins.

#1958
Q: In what city did the Romans use verdigris in murals?
Gold: Pompeii
Answer: The Romans used verdigris in the murals of Pompeii. This ancient Roman city, known for its well-preserved architecture and artifacts, served as a canvas for decorative arts, including the use of verdigris, a green pigment made from copper, brass, or bronze. 

### References

- [1] Verdigris is made by placing a plate or blade of copper, brass or bronze, slightly warmed, into a vat of fermenting wine, leaving it there for several weeks, and then scraping off and drying the green powder that forms on the metal. The process of making verdigris was described in ancient times by Pliny. It was used by the Romans in the murals of Pompeii, and in Celtic medieval manuscripts as early as the 5th century AD. It produced a blue-green which no other pigment could imitate, but it had drawbacks; it was unstable, it could not resist dampness, it did not mix well with other colors, it could ruin other colors with which it came into contact., and it was toxic. Leonardo da Vinci, in his treatise on painting, warned artists not to use it. It was widely used in miniature paintings in Europe and Persia in the 16th and 17th centuries. Its use largely ended in the late 19th century, when it was replaced by the safer and more stable chrome green. Viridian, also called chrome green, is a pigment made with chromium oxide dihydrate, was patented in 1859. It became popular with painters, since, unlike other synthetic greens, it was stable and not toxic. Vincent van Gogh used it, along with Prussian blue, to create a dark blue sky with a greenish tint in his painting Cafe terrace at night.

#1966
Q: Who can be authorized to grant assent by letters patent?
Gold: the sovereign or by Lords Commissioners
Answer: According to the Royal Assent Act 1967, royal assent can be granted by the sovereign in writing, by means of letters patent. These letters patent are presented to the presiding officer of each house of parliament. The presiding officer then makes a formal, but simple statement to the house, acquainting each house that royal assent has been granted to the acts mentioned. This method does not require both houses to meet jointly for the purpose of receiving the notice of royal assent.

### References

- [1] Under the Royal Assent Act 1967, royal assent can be granted by the sovereign in writing, by means of letters patent, that are presented to the presiding officer of each house of parliament. Then, the presiding officer makes a formal, but simple statement to the house, acquainting each house that royal assent has been granted to the acts mentioned. Thus, unlike the granting of royal assent by the monarch in person or by Royal Commissioners, the method created by the Royal Assent Act 1967 does not require both houses to meet jointly for the purpose of receiving the notice of royal assent. The standard text of the letters patent is set out in The Crown Office (Forms and Proclamations Rules) Order 1992, with minor amendments in 2000. In practice this remains the standard method, a fact that is belied by the wording of the letters patent for the appointment of the Royal Commissioners and by the wording of the letters patent for the granting of royal assent in writing under the 1967 Act (\"... And forasmuch as We cannot at this time be present in the Higher House of Our said Parliament being the accustomed place for giving Our Royal Assent...\").

Gold: a surplus of food
Answer: The advancement of agriculture made several significant changes possible, including the growth of settlements and the development of permanent dwellings. As mentioned in the knowledge base, the increased need to spend more time tending crop fields required more localized dwellings, which encouraged the growth of settlements. Additionally, the surplus of food produced from cultivated lands allowed for the support of individuals who could engage in tasks other than bare survival, such as systematic studies of nature and the development of writing (Reference [1]).

### References

- [1] A significant and far-reaching shift in human subsistence and lifestyle was to be brought about in areas where crop farming and cultivation were first developed: the previous reliance on an essentially nomadic hunter-gatherer subsistence technique or pastoral transhumance was at first supplemented, and then increasingly replaced by, a reliance upon the foods produced from cultivated lands. These developments are also believed to have greatly encouraged the growth of settlements, since it may be supposed that the increased need to spend more time and labor in tending crop fields required more localized dwellings. This trend would continue into the Bronze Age, eventually giving rise to permanently settled farming towns, and later cities and states whose larger populations could be sustained by the increased productivity from cultivated lands.

Gold: the biological status of the species
Answer: The 1982 amendment to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) changed the criteria for listing species by explicitly stating that determinations regarding the status of species must be "based solely on the best scientific and commercial data available." This modification was made to prevent any consideration of economic factors during the listing process.

### References

- [1] During the listing process, economic factors cannot be considered, but must be "based solely on the best scientific and commercial data available." The 1982 amendment to the ESA added the word "solely" to prevent any consideration other than the biological status of the species. Congress rejected President Ronald Reagan's Executive Order 12291 which required economic analysis of all government agency actions. The House committee's statement was "that economic considerations have no relevance to determinations regarding the status of species."

#1989
Q: What did St. Augustine comment on in Book 11, regarding thinking about time?
Gold: the difficulty
Answer: In Book 11 of St. Augustine's *Confessions*, he reflects deeply on the nature of time. Augustine begins by stating, "What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not." He acknowledges the difficulty in defining time, noting that while we can speak accurately about many things, "of most things we speak improperly, still the things intended are understood." Augustine further elaborates that our understanding of time is tied to the movement of things, asserting that "knowledge of time depends on the knowledge of the movement of things, and therefore time cannot be where there are no creatures to measure its passing." This passage highlights Augustine's philosophical inquiry into the nature of time and his argument for the reality of creation based on the concept of time.

### References

- [1] In Book 11 of St. Augustine's Confessions, he ruminates on the nature of time, asking, "What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not." He goes on to comment on the difficulty of thinking about time, pointing out the inaccuracy of common speech: "For but few things are there of which we speak properly; of most things we speak improperly, still the things intended are understood." But Augustine presented the first philosophical argument for the reality of Creation (against Aristotle) in the context of his discussion of time, saying that knowledge of time depends on the knowledge of the movement of things, and therefore time cannot be where there are no creatures to measure its passing (Confessions Book XI ¶30; City of God Book XI ch.6).

#2016
Q: What exactly does this system compensate for?
Gold: the differing weight of cable between the hoist and the cab
Answer: The system being referred to is the **Compensation System** used in elevators. This mechanism operates within the **Hoist-Way**, the vertical shaft in which the elevator travels, to balance the weight difference between the elevator cab and the counterweight. By doing so, it makes it easier to control the elevator. Specifically, the compensation system uses a separate set of cables or a chain attached to the bottom of the counterweight and the bottom of the elevator cab. When the elevator cab is at the top of the hoist-way, there is a short length of hoist cable above the car and a long length of compensating cable below the car. Conversely, for the counterweight, the situation is reversed. This arrangement helps in balancing the load, thereby reducing the motor's workload.

### References

- [1] Elevators with more than 30 m (98 ft) of travel have a system called compensation. This is a separate set of cables or a chain attached to the bottom of the counterweight and the bottom of the elevator cab. This makes it easier to control the elevator, as it compensates for the differing weight of cable between the hoist and the cab. If the elevator cab is at the top of the hoist-way, there is a short length of hoist cable above the car and a long length of compensating cable below the car and vice versa for the counterweight. If the compensation system uses cables, there will be an additional sheave in the pit below the elevator, to guide the cables. If the compensation system uses chains, the chain is guided by a bar mounted between the counterweight railway lines.

Q: Which  Alexander Archipenko piece was similar to other Cubist scupltures of that time?
Gold: Woman Walking
Answer: Alexander Archipenko's sculpture "Woman Walking" (1912–13) is a notable example that shares characteristics with other Cubist sculptures of that time. This piece, like others of the period, employs positive/negative space reversals, a technique that was ambitiously exploited in Cubist sculpture. For instance, Archipenko's "Woman Walking" demonstrates this technique, making it a significant contribution to the Cubist movement alongside works by other artists such as Raymond Duchamp-Villon, Jacques Lipchitz, and Ossip Zadkine, who joined the movement in 1914.

### References

- [1] Cubist sculpture developed in parallel to Cubist painting. During the autumn of 1909 Picasso sculpted Head of a Woman (Fernande) with positive features depicted by negative space and vice versa. According to Douglas Cooper: "The first true Cubist sculpture was Picasso's impressive Woman's Head, modeled in 1909–10, a counterpart in three dimensions to many similar analytical and faceted heads in his paintings at the time." These positive/negative reversals were ambitiously exploited by Alexander Archipenko in 1912–13, for example in Woman Walking. Joseph Csaky, after Archipenko, was the first sculptor in Paris to join the Cubists, with whom he exhibited from 1911 onwards. They were followed by Raymond Duchamp-Villon and then in 1914 by Jacques Lipchitz, Henri Laurens and Ossip Zadkine.

Q: What were the major advantages of the tantalum light filament?

Answer: The major advantages of the tantalum light filament included its higher efficiency and ability to operate at higher temperatures compared to graphitized carbon filaments. Siemens developed the tantalum lamp filament in 1902, and it was more efficient and could operate at higher temperatures due to the lower resistivity of tantalum metal compared to carbon. However, the filament had the property of gradually shortening in use, requiring large loops that tightened over time, making the lamps fragile after several hundred hours of use. Additionally, the metal filament had the tendency to break and re-weld, which would usually decrease the resistance and shorten the life of the filament.

### References

Since tantalum metal has a lower resistivity than carbon, the tantalum lamp filament was quite long and required multiple internal supports. The metal filament had the property of gradually shortening in use; the filaments were installed with large loops that tightened in use. This made lamps in use for several hundred hours quite fragile. Metal filaments had the property of breaking and re-welding, though this would usually decrease resistance and shorten the life of the filament. General Electric bought the rights to use tantalum filaments and produced them in the US until 1913.

#2077
Q: How is the energy stored by pumped-storage hydroelectricity recovered?
Gold: by releasing the water, with the pump becoming a hydroelectric power generator
Answer: In pumped-storage hydroelectricity, energy is stored by pumping water from a lower elevation reservoir to a higher elevation one when energy is available. During times of high demand, the stored water is released, and the pump becomes a hydroelectric power generator, converting the potential energy of the water back into electrical energy. This process allows for efficient energy storage and recovery, making it a valuable component in renewable energy systems.

### References

- [1] Pumped-storage hydroelectricity stores energy in the form of water pumped when energy is available from a lower elevation reservoir to a higher elevation one. The energy is recovered when demand is high by releasing the water, with the pump becoming a hydroelectric power generator.

Q: What can be added to allow for an antenna shorter than the needed height to produce desired results?
Gold: loading coil
Answer: To allow for an antenna shorter than the needed height to produce desired results, a loading coil can be added. This coil effectively lengthens the electrical length of the antenna, making it function as if it were the full quarter-wavelength length. However, this comes with the trade-off that the resistive impedance achieved will be quite a bit lower than that of a resonant monopole, often requiring further impedance matching. Additionally, the reactance becomes higher as the antenna size is reduced, and the resonant circuit formed by the antenna and the tuning coil has a Q factor that rises, potentially causing the bandwidth of the antenna to be inadequate for the signal being transmitted.

### References

- [1] An antenna transmits and receives radio waves with a particular polarization which can be reoriented by tilting the axis of the antenna in many (but not all) cases. The physical size of an antenna is often a practical issue, particularly at lower frequencies (longer wavelengths). Highly directional antennas need to be significantly larger than the wavelength. Resonant antennas usually use a linear conductor (or element), or pair of such elements, each of which is about a quarter of the wavelength in length (an odd multiple of quarter wavelengths will also be resonant). Antennas that are required to be small compared to the wavelength sacrifice efficiency and cannot be very directional. Fortunately at higher frequencies (UHF, microwaves) trading off performance to obtain a smaller physical size is usually not required.

The Scientific Revolution marked a transition from the traditional Aristotelian framework to a more modern scientific approach. This shift was evident in how universities began to construct their education, placing science at a higher level of importance.

For instance, the university became a context where humanism and scientific discovery were closely intertwined. Scholars like Melanchthon and his disciples at the University of Wittenberg played a crucial role in integrating new scientific ideas, such as Copernican mathematical constructs, into astronomical debate and instruction. Similarly, the adoption of Cartesian epistemology and methodology in European universities, although short-lived, demonstrated an openness to change and the integration of new scientific approaches.

These changes indicated a move away from the traditional, Aristotelian framework towards a more mechanistic and empirical approach to understanding the natural world. The autonomy of science began to emerge, leading to a hierarchy of disciplines where science was increasingly seen as a vocation in itself, distinct from the general scholar's training.

### References

- [1] The Scientific Revolution was a period when European ideas in classical physics, astronomy, biology, human anatomy, chemistry, and other classical sciences were rejected and led to doctrines supplanting those that had prevailed from Ancient Greece to the Middle Ages which would lead to a transition to modern science.
- [2] Other historians find incongruity in the proposition that the very place where the vast number of the scholars that influenced the scientific revolution received their education should also be the place that inhibits their research and the advancement of science. In fact, more than 80% of the European scientists between 1450–1650 included in the Dictionary of Scientific Biography were university trained, of which approximately 45% held university posts.
- [3] By the end of the early modern period, the structure and orientation of higher education had changed in ways that are eminently recognizable for the modern context. Q: What sort of synthesis occurs when the RNA molecules are the actual functional products?
Gold: the synthesis of ribosomal RNA and transfer RNA
Answer: When RNA molecules serve as the actual functional products, they are involved in processes other than the synthesis of proteins. For instance, ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and transfer RNA (tRNA) are examples of RNA molecules that are not translated into proteins but play crucial roles in protein synthesis. Specifically, rRNA is a key component of the ribosome, the cellular machinery responsible for protein synthesis, while tRNA carries amino acids to the ribosome during translation.

Another example of RNA molecules that function directly is ribozymes, which are RNA molecules capable of performing enzymatic functions. These ribozymes can catalyze various biochemical reactions without the need for protein enzymes.

Q: When was the treaty to regulate mining agreed upon?
Gold: 1988
Answer: The treaty to regulate mining in Antarctica was agreed upon in 1988. Specifically, the Convention on the Regulation of Antarctic Mineral Resources (CRAMRA) was adopted in 1988. However, it was not ratified by key countries, and thus it was rendered effectively dead. Subsequently, a comprehensive environmental protection regime, the Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty (the "Madrid Protocol"), was negotiated and entered into force on 14 January 1998, which banned all mining in Antarctica.

### References

- [1] In 1983, the Antarctic Treaty Parties began negotiations on a convention to regulate mining in Antarctica. A coalition of international organizations launched a public pressure campaign to prevent any minerals development in the region, led largely by Greenpeace International, which established its own scientific station—World Park Base—in the Ross Sea region and conducted annual expeditions to document environmental effects of humans on Antarctica. In 1988, the Convention on the Regulation of Antarctic Mineral Resources (CRAMRA) was adopted. The following year, however, Australia and France announced that they would not ratify the convention, rendering it dead for all intents and purposes. They proposed instead that a comprehensive regime to protect the Antarctic environment be negotiated in its place. The Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty (the "Madrid Protocol") was negotiated as other countries followed suit and on 14 January 1998 it entered into force. The Madrid Protocol bans all mining in Antarctica, designating Antarctica a "natural reserve devoted to peace and science."

#2247
Q: What are dynamic range neurons?
Gold: spinal cord fibers
Answer: Dynamic range neurons, also known as wide dynamic range neurons, are spinal cord neurons that respond to a variety of sensory inputs, including A-delta and C fibers, as well as large A-beta fibers. These neurons play a crucial role in transmitting pain signals from nociceptors to the brain. A-delta fibers are responsible for transmitting sharp, quick pain, while C fibers are involved in transmitting dull, aching pain. Large A-beta fibers carry touch, pressure, and vibration signals. The wide dynamic range of these neurons allows them to process both painful and non-painful stimuli, making them essential for the proper functioning of the spinal cord in pain signal transmission.

### References

- [1] Spinal Cord
- [2] Wide Dynamic Range Neurons

Q: What is a discrete transistor?
Gold: individually packaged transistors
Answer: A discrete transistor is an individually packaged semiconductor device used in electronic circuits. These transistors come in various semiconductor packages, with the two main categories being through-hole (or leaded) and surface-mount, also known as surface-mount device (SMD). ### References

- [1] Discrete transistors are individually packaged transistors. Transistors come in many different semiconductor packages (see image). The two main categories are through-hole (or leaded), and surface-mount, also known as surface-mount device (SMD). The ball grid array (BGA) is the latest surface-mount package (currently only for large integrated circuits). It has solder "balls" on the underside in place of leads. Because they are smaller and have shorter interconnections, SMDs have better high-frequency characteristics but lower power rating.

Q: What did Whitehead ask people to reimagine in order for philosophy to make progress?

Answer: Whitehead believed that people need to continually re-imagine their basic assumptions about the universe for progress in philosophy and science. He argued that scientists and philosophers make metaphysical assumptions about how the universe works all the time, but such assumptions are often unexamined and unquestioned. Whitehead maintained that these assumptions should be continually re-examined to foster genuine progress. According to his views, even if such progress remains asymptotic, the process of reimagining these fundamental assumptions is essential for both good science and good philosophy.

### References

- [1] Whitehead was quoted as saying: "Every scientific man in order to preserve his reputation has to say he dislikes metaphysics. What he means is he dislikes having his metaphysics criticized." In Whitehead's view, scientists and philosophers make metaphysical assumptions about how the universe works all the time, but such assumptions are not easily seen precisely because they remain unexamined and unquestioned. While Whitehead acknowledged that "philosophers can never hope finally to formulate these metaphysical first principles," he argued that people need to continually re-imagine their basic assumptions about how the universe works if philosophy and science are to make any real progress, even if that progress remains permanently asymptotic. For this reason Whitehead regarded metaphysical investigations as essential to both good science and good philosophy.

With the outbreak of World War I, the modernization process stopped abruptly. The Ottoman aviation squadrons fought on many fronts during World War I, from Galicia in the west to the Caucasus in the east and Yemen in the south.

Q: How do enhancers increase transcription?
Gold: by binding an activator protein
Answer: Enhancers increase transcription by binding to activator proteins, which then help recruit RNA polymerase to the promoter. Specifically, enhancers are DNA sequences that increase the transcription of a gene by binding activator proteins. These activator proteins are transcription factors that enhance gene expression by binding to enhancers. The binding of activator proteins to enhancers causes the DNA to loop, bringing the regulatory sequence and the bound transcription factor closer to the RNA polymerase binding site. This proximity facilitates the initiation of transcription by RNA polymerase.

### References

- [1] Additionally, genes can have regulatory regions many kilobases upstream or downstream of the open reading frame. These act by binding to transcription factors which then cause the DNA to loop so that the regulatory sequence (and bound transcription factor) become close to the RNA polymerase binding site. For example, enhancers increase transcription by binding an activator protein which then helps to recruit the RNA polymerase to the promoter; conversely silencers bind repressor proteins and make the DNA less available for RNA polymerase.

Q: What type of support did child give to their families by working?

Answer: During the colonial period, children often worked to support their families through various means. Colonial administrators encouraged traditional kin-ordered modes of production, which involved hiring entire households, including children, for work. This practice allowed children to contribute to their family's income and well-being. Additionally, sophisticated schemes like the Pauper Apprenticeship were implemented, where children could be assigned to labor away from their parents at distant farms owned by different colonial masters without the need for parental consent. These arrangements ensured that children could contribute to their family's economic needs, even if it meant being separated from their parents.

Q: Lieberman and Jackson suggest authors of some studies use the term race in what ways?
Gold: conceptually imprecise and careless
Answer: Lieberman and Jackson argue that studies using the term race are conceptually imprecise and careless. They claim that these studies find support for racial distinctions only because they began by assuming the validity of race. Instead, they suggest emphasizing clinal variation and adaptive human hereditary variation, which recognizes the existence of genetic diversity without the rigid categorization implied by the term "race."

### References

- [1] For the anthropologists Lieberman and Jackson (1995), however, there are more profound methodological and conceptual problems with using cladistics to support concepts of race. They claim that "the molecular and biochemical proponents of this model explicitly use racial categories in their initial grouping of samples." For example, the large and highly diverse macroethnic groups of East Indians, North Africans, and Europeans are presumptively grouped as Caucasians prior to the analysis of their DNA variation. This is claimed to limit and skew interpretations, obscure other lineage relationships, deemphasize the impact of more immediate clinal environmental factors on genomic diversity, and can cloud our understanding of the true patterns of affinity. They argue that however significant the empirical research, these studies use the term race in conceptually imprecise and careless ways. They suggest that the authors of these studies find support for racial distinctions only because they began by assuming the validity of race. "For empirical reasons we prefer to place emphasis on clinal variation, which recognizes the existence of adaptive human hereditary variation and simultaneously stresses that such variation is not found in packages that can be labeled races."

#2405
Q: The invariant interval that separates two events in Minkowski spacetime can either be what?
Gold: space-like, light-like, or time-like
Answer: The invariant interval that separates two events in Minkowski spacetime can either be space-like, light-like, or time-like. Specifically, events that have a time-like separation cannot be simultaneous in any frame of reference, while events that have a space-like separation will be simultaneous in some frame of reference. The invariant interval remains the same for all observers, regardless of their velocity, making it a fundamental concept in the formulation of special relativity within Minkowski spacetime.

### References

- [1] The theory of special relativity finds a convenient formulation in Minkowski spacetime, a mathematical structure that combines three dimensions of space with a single dimension of time. In this formalism, distances in space can be measured by how long light takes to travel that distance, e.g., a light-year is a measure of distance, and a meter is now defined in terms of how far light travels in a certain amount of time. Two events in Minkowski spacetime are separated by an invariant interval, which can be either space-like, light-like, or time-like. Events that have a time-like separation cannot be simultaneous in any frame of reference, there must be a temporal component (and possibly a spatial one) to their separation. Events that have a space-like separation will be simultaneous in some frame of reference, and there is no frame of reference in which they do not have a spatial separation. Different observers may calculate different distances and different time intervals between two events, but the invariant interval between the events is independent of the observer (and his velocity).

#2408
Q: What component was to blame for the weak bass of the 3rd generation iPod?
Gold: undersized DC-blocking capacitors
Answer: The weak bass response issue in the third-generation iPod was primarily due to the use of undersized DC-blocking capacitors. These capacitors, when combined with the typical low-impedance of most consumer headphones, form a high-pass filter that attenuates the low-frequency bass output.

### References

- [1] The third-generation iPod had a weak bass response, as shown in audio tests. The combination of the undersized DC-blocking capacitors and the typical low-impedance of most consumer headphones form a high-pass filter, which attenuates the low-frequency bass output. Similar capacitors were used in the fourth-generation iPods. The problem is reduced when using high-impedance headphones and is completely masked when driving high-impedance (line level) loads, such as an external headphone amplifier. The first-generation iPod Shuffle uses a dual-transistor output stage, rather than a single capacitor-coupled output, and does not exhibit reduced bass response for any load.

Q: What type of drugs can impair the judgement of time?
Gold: Psychoactive drugs
Answer: Psychoactive drugs can impair the judgment of time. Specifically, stimulants can lead both humans and rats to overestimate time intervals, while depressants can have the opposite effect, causing humans to underestimate time intervals. This effect is thought to be due to the alteration in the firing rate of neurons in the brain, which can either excite or inhibit the brain's capacity to distinguish events occurring within a given interval.

### References

The level of activity in the brain of neurotransmitters such as dopamine and norepinephrine may be the reason for this. Such chemicals will either excite or inhibit the firing of neurons in the brain, with a greater firing rate allowing the brain to register the occurrence of more events within a given interval (speed up time) and a decreased firing rate reducing the brain's capacity to distinguish events occurring within a given interval (slow down time).

Answer: Divan poetry was based on a strict metrical framework, which allowed for the juxtaposition of many images and symbols, thereby creating multiple potential meanings. This framework inherited symbols from Persian poetry, which were used to convey complex and nuanced ideas.

### References

- [1] Ottoman Divan poetry was a highly ritualized and symbolic art form. From the Persian poetry that largely inspired it, it inherited a wealth of symbols whose meanings and interrelationships—both of similitude (مراعات نظير mura'ât-i nazîr / تناسب tenâsüb) and opposition (تضاد tezâd) were more or less prescribed. Divan poetry was composed through the constant juxtaposition of many such images within a strict metrical framework, thus allowing numerous potential meanings to emerge. The vast majority of Divan poetry was lyric in nature: either gazels (which make up the greatest part of the repertoire of the tradition), or kasîdes. There were, however, other common genres, most particularly the mesnevî, a kind of verse romance and thus a variety of narrative poetry; the two most notable examples of this form are the Leyli and Majnun of Fuzûlî and the Hüsn ü Aşk of Şeyh Gâlib.

#2437
Q: What is the goal of the textual critic?
Gold: a "critical edition"
Answer: The goal of the textual critic is to produce a "critical edition" that accurately represents the original text. This edition is accompanied by an apparatus criticus or critical apparatus, which provides detailed information about the textual evidence. The critical apparatus includes three main components: a list or description of the evidence used by the editor, the editor's analysis of that evidence, and a record of rejected variants of the text.

### References

- [1] The textual critic's ultimate objective is the production of a "critical edition" which contains the text that the author has determined most closely approximates the original, and is accompanied by an apparatus criticus or critical apparatus. The critical apparatus presents the author's work in three parts: first, a list or description of the evidence that the editor used (names of manuscripts, or abbreviations called sigla); second, the editor's analysis of that evidence (sometimes a simple likelihood rating); and third, a record of rejected variants of the text (often in order of preference).

#2450
Q: What sends a point in the square to the relating point under the symmetry?
Gold: functions
Answer: In the context of the dihedral group \(D_4\), the functions representing symmetries send a point in the square to the corresponding point under the symmetry. For example, the function \(r_1\) sends a point to its rotation 90° clockwise around the square's center, and the function \(f_h\) sends a point to its reflection across the square's vertical middle line.

### References

- [1] These symmetries are represented by functions. Each of these functions sends a point in the square to the corresponding point under the symmetry. For example, \(r_1\) sends a point to its rotation 90° clockwise around the square's center, and \(f_h\) sends a point to its reflection across the square's vertical middle line. Composing two of these symmetry functions gives another symmetry function. These symmetries determine a group called the dihedral group of degree 4 and denoted \(D_4\). The underlying set of the group is the above set of symmetry functions, and the group operation is function composition. Two symmetries are combined by composing them as functions, that is, applying the first one to the square, and the second one to the result of the first application.

#2452
Q: How was Mayor Bertand Delanoe elected
Gold: majority of council members
Answer: Mayor Bertrand Delanoë was elected as the mayor of Paris from 2001 to 2014. He was elected by a minority of city voters but received the support of a majority of the Council of Paris (Conseil de Paris) members. The Council of Paris, composed of 163 members, is indirectly elected by the voters of each arrondissement (administrative division) in Paris. Each arrondissement has a number of members depending on its population, ranging from 10 members for the least-populated arrondissements (1st through 9th) to 36 members for the most populated (the 15th). Once elected, the council plays a largely passive role in the city government, meeting only once a month. The elected council members then select the mayor.

### References

- [1] The mayor of Paris is elected indirectly by Paris voters; the voters of each arrondissement elect the Conseil de Paris (Council of Paris), composed of 163 members. Each arrondissement has a number of members depending upon its population, from 10 members for each of the least-populated arrondissements (1st through 9th) to 36 members for the most populated (the 15th). The elected council members select the mayor. Sometimes the candidate who receives the most votes city-wide is not selected if the other candidate has won the support of the majority of council members. Mayor Bertrand Delanoë (2001-2014) was elected by only a minority of city voters, but a majority of council members.

Q: What did KInsey find during these studies ?
Gold: that when the individuals' behavior as well as their identity are analyzed, most people appeared to be at least somewhat bisexual
Answer: Alfred C. Kinsey and his team conducted extensive research on human sexuality, as detailed in their seminal works, "Sexual Behavior in the Human Male" (1948) and "Sexual Behavior in the Human Female" (1953). Kinsey found that most people exhibit some degree of bisexuality, meaning they have some attraction to both sexes, although one sex is usually preferred. According to Kinsey, only a minority of individuals (5-10%) can be considered fully heterosexual or homosexual. Kinsey's research involved asking individuals to rate themselves on a scale from completely heterosexual to completely homosexual, considering both their behavior and identity. However, his methods have been criticized for potential flaws, particularly regarding the randomness of his sample population, which included prison inmates, male prostitutes, and those who willingly participated in discussions of previously taboo sexual topics. Despite these criticisms, Kinsey's work introduced a more nuanced understanding of sexual orientation, challenging the traditional dichotomy of homosexuality and heterosexuality.

- [2] Sexual Behavior in the Human Female

#2471
Q: When does the Gregorian calendar omit 3 leap days?
Gold: every 400 years
Answer: The Gregorian calendar omits 3 leap days every 400 years. Specifically, a year that is divisible by 100 is not a leap year unless it is also divisible by 400. This rule ensures that the calendar remains aligned with the solar year.

### References

- [1] The Gregorian calendar is a solar calendar. A regular Gregorian year consists of 365 days, but as in the Julian calendar, in a leap year, a leap day is added to February. In the Julian calendar a leap year occurs every 4 years, but the Gregorian calendar omits 3 leap days every 400 years. In the Julian calendar, this leap day was inserted by doubling 24 February, and the Gregorian reform did not change the date of the leap day. In the modern period, it has become customary to number the days from the beginning of the month, and February 29th is often considered as the leap day. Some churches, notably the Roman Catholic Church, delay February festivals after the 23rd by one day in leap years.

### References

- [2] Norfolk Island was originally a colony acquired by settlement but was never within the British Settlements Act. In 1976 the High Court of Australia held unanimously that Norfolk Island is a part of the Commonwealth. Again, in 2007 the High Court of Australia affirmed the validity of legislation that made Australian citizenship a necessary qualification for voting for, and standing for election to, the Legislative Assembly of Norfolk Island.

#2487
Q: What trait does Old English possess that Modern English lacks?
Gold: morphological diversity
Answer: Old English possesses a trait of **rich morphological diversity** that is largely absent in Modern English. According to the knowledge graph, Old English maintained several distinct cases: the nominative, accusative, genitive, dative, and (vestigially) instrumental. These cases were used to indicate the grammatical function of nouns and their modifying words, depending on their case. In contrast, Modern English retains only a few remnants of this system, primarily in the forms of a few pronouns (such as I/me/mine, she/her, who/whom/whose) and in the possessive ending -'s, which derives from the old (masculine and neuter) genitive ending -es.

### References

- [1] Old English (Ænglisc, Anglisc, Englisc) is the earliest historical form of the English language, spoken in England and southern and eastern Scotland in the early Middle Ages. It was brought to Great Britain by Anglo-Saxon settlers probably in the mid 5th century, and the first Old English literary works date from the mid 7th century.
- [2] Unlike Modern English, Old English is a language rich in morphological diversity. It maintains several distinct cases: the nominative, accusative, genitive, dative and (vestigially) instrumental. The only remnants of this system in Modern English are in the forms of a few pronouns (such as I/me/mine, she/her, who/whom/whose) and in the possessive ending -'s, which derives from the old (masculine and neuter) genitive ending -es.

#2496
Q: Which pramanas is understanding of experts?
Gold: śabda
Answer: The term "pramanas" refers to the means of knowledge or epistemic sources in Indian epistemology. In the context of understanding experts, pramanas can be understood as the reliable methods or sources through which experts derive their knowledge and insights. These pramanas include:

- **Testimony (Anumana)**: This involves accepting the knowledge conveyed by reliable sources, such as experts in their respective fields. Experts often rely on the testimony of other experts or established knowledge bases to build their understanding.

- **Inference (Anumana)**: Experts use logical reasoning and inference to derive new knowledge from existing data or observations. This is a key method by which experts extend their understanding beyond direct experience.

- **Perception (Pratyaksha)**: Direct observation and experience are crucial for experts, especially in fields where empirical evidence is paramount. For instance, a medical expert might rely on direct observation of symptoms to diagnose a patient.

- **Scriptural Testimony (Shabda)**: In some fields, experts might rely on authoritative texts or scriptures that provide foundational knowledge. For example, in traditional medicine, texts like the Ayurveda might be considered authoritative.

- **Reasoning (Yukti)**: Logical reasoning and critical thinking are essential for experts to formulate and validate their hypotheses and theories.

Understanding experts involves recognizing the role of these pramanas in their knowledge acquisition and application. Each pramana plays a critical role in the epistemic process, ensuring that the knowledge derived is reliable and valid.

- [1] Document Title One
- [2] Document Title Two
- [3] Document Title Three

#2500
Q: Were Laserdiscs initially cheaper or more costly to produce than their VHS counterparts?
Gold: cheaper
Answer: LaserDiscs were initially cheaper to produce than VHS videocassettes. This was due to the simpler manufacturing process of LaserDiscs, which lacked the moving parts and plastic outer shell required for VHS tapes. However, by the end of the 1980s, the average disc-pressing prices for LaserDiscs had increased to over $5.00 per two-sided disc, primarily due to the large amount of plastic material and the costly glass-mastering process needed to make the metal stamper mechanisms. In contrast, the volume of demand for videocassettes led to a significant decrease in their duplication costs, with some sources indicating that by the beginning of the 1990s, duplicating a VHS tape could cost as little as $1.00.

### References

- [1] LaserDiscs were initially cheaper than videocassettes to manufacture, because they lacked the moving parts and plastic outer shell that are necessary for VHS tapes to work, and the duplication process was much simpler. A VHS cassette has at least 14 parts including the actual tape while LaserDisc has one part with five or six layers. A disc can be stamped out in a matter of seconds whereas duplicating videotape required a complex bulk tape duplication mechanism and was a time-consuming process. However, by the end of the 1980s, average disc-pressing prices were over $5.00 per two-sided disc, due to the large amount of plastic material and the costly glass-mastering process needed to make the metal stamper mechanisms. Due to the larger volume of demand, videocassettes quickly became much cheaper to duplicate, costing as little as $1.00 by the beginning of the 1990s.

#2504
Q: Australia was connected to which other continent at the start of the Eocene?
Gold: Antarctica
Answer: At the beginning of the Eocene period, Australia was connected to Antarctica. This connection played a significant role in the climate and ocean currents of the region, as the warm equatorial currents mixed with colder Antarctic waters, distributing heat around the world and maintaining high global temperatures (Reference ID: ).

### References

- [1] During the Eocene (56 million years ago - 33.9 million years ago), the continents continued to drift toward their present positions. At the beginning of the period, Australia and Antarctica remained connected, and warm equatorial currents mixed with colder Antarctic waters, distributing the heat around the world and keeping global temperatures high. But when Australia split from the southern continent around 45 Ma, the warm equatorial currents were deflected away from Antarctica, and an isolated cold water channel developed between the two continents. The Antarctic region cooled down, and the ocean surrounding Antarctica began to freeze, sending cold water and ice floes north, reinforcing the cooling. The present pattern of ice ages began about 40 million years ago.[citation needed]

### References

- [1] Among predators there is a large degree of specialization. Many predators specialize in hunting only one species of prey. Others are more opportunistic and will kill and eat almost anything (examples: humans, leopards, dogs and alligators). The specialists are usually particularly well suited to capturing their preferred prey. The prey in turn, are often equally suited to escape that predator. This is called an evolutionary arms race and tends to keep the populations of both species in equilibrium. Some predators specialize in certain classes of prey, not just single species. Some will switch to other prey (with varying degrees of success) when the preferred target is extremely scarce, and they may also resort to scavenging or a herbivorous diet if possible.

Q: What is known about the light absorption of a hot object in equilibrium with light?
Gold: absorbs just as much light as it emits
Answer: A hot object in thermal equilibrium with light, such as a black object, absorbs all the light that hits it, maximizing its thermal light emission. This is a fundamental property of black objects, which are ideal for maximizing the absorption and subsequent emission of thermal radiation. The Stefan–Boltzmann law, which accurately predicts the total amount of emitted energy from black-body radiation, is directly applicable to such objects. Additionally, the brightness of a hot object depends on its temperature, with higher temperatures leading to greater light emission.

### References

It is well known that hot objects glow, and that hotter objects glow brighter than cooler ones. The electromagnetic field obeys laws of motion similarly to a mass on a spring, and can come to thermal equilibrium with hot atoms. The hot object in equilibrium with light absorbs just as much light as it emits. If the object is black, meaning it absorbs all the light that hits it, then its thermal light emission is maximized.

#2578
Q: What is the photoelectric effect?
Gold: the emission of electrons (called "photoelectrons") from a surface when light is shone on it
Answer: The photoelectric effect is a phenomenon where electrons are emitted from a surface when light is shone on it. This effect was first observed by Alexandre Edmond Becquerel in 1839, although credit is usually reserved for Heinrich Hertz, who published the first thorough investigation in 1887. Another significant contribution was made by Philipp Lenard in 1902. Albert Einstein provided a theoretical explanation of the photoelectric effect in terms of light quanta (photons) in 1905, which earned him the Nobel Prize in 1921 when his predictions were confirmed by the experimental work of Robert Andrews Millikan.

### References

- [1] The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons (called "photoelectrons") from a surface when light is shone on it. It was first observed by Alexandre Edmond Becquerel in 1839, although credit is usually reserved for Heinrich Hertz, who published the first thorough investigation in 1887. Another particularly thorough investigation was published by Philipp Lenard in 1902. Einstein's 1905 paper discussing the effect in terms of light quanta would earn him the Nobel Prize in 1921, when his predictions had been confirmed by the experimental work of Robert Andrews Millikan. The Nobel committee awarded the prize for his work on the photo-electric effect, rather than relativity, both because of a bias against purely theoretical physics not grounded in discovery or experiment, and dissent amongst its members as to the actual proof that relativity was real.

#2608
Q: What are three digestions phases?
Gold: the cephalic phase , gastric phase, and intestinal phase
Answer: The human digestive system involves three main phases of digestion: the cephalic phase, the gastric phase, and the intestinal phase.

1. **Cephalic Phase**: This phase begins even before food enters the mouth. It is initiated by the sight, thought, and smell of food, which stimulate the cerebral cortex. Taste and smell stimuli are sent to the hypothalamus and medulla oblongata, and from there, through the vagus nerve, acetylcholine is released. This stimulates gastric secretion to 40% of its maximum rate, although at this point, the stomach is not yet exposed to food and thus does not buffer acidity, which helps inhibit parietal and G cell activity via D cell secretion of somatostatin.

2. **Gastric Phase**: This phase is stimulated by the presence of food in the stomach, distension of the stomach, and a decrease in pH. As food enters the stomach, it triggers the release of gastric juices, which include hydrochloric acid and pepsin. The stomach's peristaltic movements mix the food with these digestive juices. The gastric phase lasts approximately 3 to 4 hours and involves the release of gastrin by G cells, which stimulates parietal cells to secrete gastric acid.

3. **Intestinal Phase**: This phase has two parts: the excitatory and the inhibitory. Partially digested food in the duodenum stimulates the release of intestinal gastrin. The enterogastric reflex inhibits vagal nuclei, activates sympathetic fibers, causing the pyloric sphincter to tighten to prevent more food from entering, and inhibits local reflexes. This phase is crucial for the further breakdown and absorption of nutrients.

- [1] Document Title One
- [2] Document Title Two
- [3] Document Title Three

However, it is important to note that while the Roman Catholic Church holds this belief, Orthodox Christians reject the Immaculate Conception due to differences in their understanding of ancestral sin.

#2678
Q: What is considered to be central to the teachings of Buddhism?
Gold: the Four Noble Truths
Answer: Central to the teachings of Buddhism are the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path. The Four Noble Truths, which are fundamental to Buddhist thought, provide a conceptual framework for understanding the nature of suffering (dukkha) and its cessation. These truths are:

1. The truth of suffering (dukkha): Suffering is an inherent part of life.
2. The truth of the origin of suffering: Suffering arises from craving and ignorance.
3. The truth of the cessation of suffering: Suffering can be overcome.
4. The truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering: The Noble Eightfold Path.

The Noble Eightfold Path, as the fourth of the Buddha's Noble Truths, consists of eight interconnected factors or conditions that, when developed together, lead to the cessation of suffering. These factors are: Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration.

These teachings are essential for understanding and following the Buddhist path, and they are based on the Three Jewels: the Buddha, the Dharma (the teachings), and the Sangha (the community).

### References

- [1] The teachings on the Four Noble Truths are regarded as central to the teachings of Buddhism, and are said to provide a conceptual framework for Buddhist thought.
- [2] The Noble Eightfold Path—the fourth of the Buddha's Noble Truths—consists of a set of eight interconnected factors or conditions, that when developed together, lead to the cessation of dukkha.

Q: ACLs and capability based security are two security models capable of what?
Gold: enforcing privilege separation
Answer: Access Control Lists (ACLs) and capability-based security are two security models capable of enforcing privilege separation in computer systems. However, ACLs can be insecure due to the confused deputy problem and the inability to guarantee access to an object to only one person, which is a security flaw. Capability-based security resolves these issues by addressing the confused deputy problem and the inability to guarantee access to an object to only one person.

### References

- [1] Within computer systems, two of many security models capable of enforcing privilege separation are access control lists (ACLs) and capability-based security. Using ACLs to confine programs has been proven to be insecure in many situations, such as if the host computer can be tricked into indirectly allowing restricted file access, an issue known as the confused deputy problem. It has also been shown that the promise of ACLs of giving access to an object to only one person can never be guaranteed in practice. Both of these problems are resolved by capabilities. This does not mean practical flaws exist in all ACL-based systems, but only that the designers of certain utilities must take responsibility to ensure that they do not introduce flaws.

Q: What can be learned from the study of modern hunter-gatherers?
Gold: nothing meaningful
Answer: The study of modern hunter-gatherers can provide valuable insights into prehistoric human societies, although this perspective is contested by some theorists who advocate a "revisionist" critique. According to these theorists, the "pure hunter-gatherer" state disappeared shortly after colonial or agricultural contact began, making modern hunter-gatherers irrelevant for understanding prehistoric societies (Kelly, 24-29; see Wilmsen).

However, many contemporary hunter-gatherer societies still exist, and they often supplement their foraging activities with horticulture and/or keeping animals. This adaptability suggests that hunting and gathering is not a static strategy but one that can be revisited under certain conditions, such as extreme food stress (Reference ID: 2). The transition from hunting and gathering to agriculture is not necessarily a one-way process, and there is often overlap between these two subsistence strategies (Reference ID: 3).

Moreover, the study of modern hunter-gatherers can contribute to our understanding of human evolution. For instance, the endurance running hypothesis posits that long-distance running, still practiced by some hunter-gatherer groups, was a driving evolutionary force in the development of certain human characteristics (Reference ID: 4).

### References

Q: How was sensitivity expressed at first in the DIN system?
Gold: as a fraction with 'tenths' (for example "18/10° DIN")
Answer: At first, sensitivity in the DIN system was expressed in 'degrees' as a fraction with 'tenths'. For example, a film speed of "18/10° DIN" represented the relative base 10 logarithm of the speed. This notation indicated that the film's sensitivity was 1.8 times the base speed.

### References

- [1] As in the Scheiner system, speeds were expressed in 'degrees'. Originally the sensitivity was written as a fraction with 'tenths' (for example "18/10° DIN"), where the resultant value 1.8 represented the relative base 10 logarithm of the speed. 'Tenths' were later abandoned with DIN 4512:1957-11, and the example above would be written as "18° DIN". The degree symbol was finally dropped with DIN 4512:1961-10. This revision also saw significant changes in the definition of film speeds in order to accommodate then-recent changes in the American ASA PH2.5-1960 standard, so that film speeds of black-and-white negative film effectively would become doubled, that is, a film previously marked as "18° DIN" would now be labeled as "21 DIN" without emulsion changes.

Q: How was the bull's-eye used?
Gold: for decorative effect
Answer: The bull's-eye, a decorative window pane with non-uniform thickness, was used in glass factories during the early twentieth century. Molten glass was poured onto a large cooling table and allowed to spread, resulting in a thicker center where the pour occurred. These sheets were then cut into smaller window panes, often with the pour location centered in one of the panes for decorative effect. This non-uniform thickness was a characteristic of traditional glass window panes produced before the advent of float glass, which is very uniform in thickness.

### References

- [1] Mass production of glass window panes in the early twentieth century caused a similar effect. In glass factories, molten glass was poured onto a large cooling table and allowed to spread. The resulting glass is thicker at the location of the pour, located at the center of the large sheet. These sheets were cut into smaller window panes with nonuniform thickness, typically with the location of the pour centered in one of the panes (known as "bull's-eyes") for decorative effect. Modern glass intended for windows is produced as float glass and is very uniform in thickness.

Q: At what rate is the drain-source current increased when the gate-source current is increased?
Gold: a roughly quadratic rate
Answer: The rate at which the drain-source current (IDS) is increased when the gate-source voltage (VGS) is increased depends on the region of operation of the field-effect transistor (FET). Below the threshold voltage, the drain-source current increases exponentially with the gate-source voltage. Once the threshold voltage is exceeded, the current increases at a roughly quadratic rate in the space-charge-limited region.

### References

- [1] In a FET, the drain–source current (IDS) increases exponentially for VGS below threshold, and then at a roughly quadratic rate (IDS ∝ (VGS − VT)²) (where VT is the threshold voltage at which drain current begins) in the "space-charge-limited" region above threshold. A quadratic behavior is not observed in modern devices, for example, at the 65 nm technology node.

#2784
Q: Besides upholding international treaty, what else have countries done specifically to digital works and uses?
Gold: enacted compulsory licensing laws
Answer: Countries have implemented various legislative measures to address digital works and uses, beyond simply upholding international treaties. For instance, the U.S. Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) of 1998 provides online intermediaries with limited statutory immunity from liability for copyright infringement. This act characterizes the limited statutory immunity provided to online intermediaries as "safe harbor" provisions, ensuring that platforms hosting content are not liable for copyright infringement if they do not know about it and take actions once the infringing content is brought to their attention.

In Europe, the European E-Commerce Directive (2000) also governs the principles of "mere conduit" and "no obligation to monitor" for Internet Service Providers (ISPs). The "mere conduit" principle means that ISPs are neutral 'pipes' with no knowledge of what they are carrying, while the "no obligation to monitor" principle means that ISPs cannot be given a general mandate by governments to monitor content. These principles serve as barriers for certain forms of online copyright enforcement.

These legislative measures aim to balance the interests of content creators and users, providing a framework for the protection and use of digital works while accommodating the rapid evolution of digital technologies.

### References

- [1] The U.S. Digital Millennium Copyright Act (1998) and the European E-Commerce Directive (2000) provide online intermediaries with limited statutory immunity from liability for copyright infringement.
- [2] The European E-Commerce Directive governs the "mere conduit" principle for Internet Service Providers.

#2787
Q: What is unique about the method used for assention allowed by the Royal Assent Act 1967?
Gold: does not require both houses to meet jointly
Answer: The Royal Assent Act 1967 introduced a unique method for granting royal assent, which is less ceremonial compared to the traditional methods. According to the Act, royal assent can be granted by the sovereign in writing, through letters patent. These letters patent are then presented to the presiding officer of each house of parliament. The presiding officer then makes a formal, but simple statement to the house, informing them that royal assent has been granted to the acts mentioned. This method does not require both houses to meet jointly for the purpose of receiving the notice of royal assent, unlike the granting of royal assent by the monarch in person or by Royal Commissioners. 

The standard text of the letters patent is set out in The Crown Office (Forms and Proclamations Rules) Order 1992, with minor amendments in 2000. In practice, this remains the standard method for granting royal assent, as evidenced by the wording of the letters patent for the appointment of the Royal Commissioners and for the granting of royal assent in writing under the 1967 Act.

### References

- [1] Under the Royal Assent Act 1967, royal assent can be granted by the sovereign in writing, by means of letters patent, that are presented to the presiding officer of each house of parliament. Then, the presiding officer makes a formal, but simple statement to the house, acquainting each house that royal assent has been granted to the acts mentioned. Thus, unlike the granting of royal assent by the monarch in person or by Royal Commissioners, the method created by the Royal Assent Act 1967 does not require both houses to meet jointly for the purpose of receiving the notice of royal assent. The standard text of the letters patent is set out in The Crown Office (Forms and Proclamations Rules) Order 1992, with minor amendments in 2000. In practice this remains the standard method, a fact that is belied by the wording of the letters patent for the appointment of the Royal Commissioners and by the wording of the letters patent for the granting of royal assent in writing under the 1967 Act (\"... And forasmuch as We cannot at this time be present in the Higher House of Our said Parliament being the accustomed place for giving Our Royal Assent...\").

#2799
Q: What causes glass to dissolve in water?
Gold: soda
Answer: Glass, particularly soda-lime glass, can dissolve in water due to the presence of certain components in its composition. Soda-lime glass contains about 70 to 74% silica by weight, along with sodium carbonate (soda) and lime (calcium oxide) added to lower the glass transition temperature and improve chemical durability. However, the soda component makes the glass water-soluble, which is usually undesirable. To counteract this, lime and other substances like magnesium oxide and aluminum oxide are added to enhance the chemical durability of the glass.

### References

- [1] Fused quartz is a glass made from chemically-pure SiO2 (silica). It has excellent thermal shock characteristics, being able to survive immersion in water while red hot. However, its high melting-temperature (1723 °C) and viscosity make it difficult to work with. Normally, other substances are added to simplify processing. One is sodium carbonate (Na2CO3, "soda"), which lowers the glass transition temperature. The soda makes the glass water-soluble, which is usually undesirable, so lime (calcium oxide [CaO], generally obtained from limestone), some magnesium oxide (MgO) and aluminium oxide (Al2O3) are added to provide for a better chemical durability. The resulting glass contains about 70 to 74% silica by weight and is called a soda-lime glass. Soda-lime glasses account for about 90% of manufactured glass.

The higher the bit rate, the larger the compressed file will be, and generally, the closer it will sound to the original file. However, at lower bit rates, the file size is reduced, but the sound quality may be noticeably lower.

Q: What methods are used to remove non-audible components of audio signals?
Gold: psychoacoustics
Answer: In lossy audio compression, methods of psychoacoustics are used to remove non-audible (or less audible) components of the audio signal. This process works by reducing the accuracy of certain parts of a sound that are considered to be beyond the auditory resolution ability of most people. This method is commonly referred to as perceptual coding. It uses psychoacoustic models to discard or reduce precision of components less audible to human hearing, and then records the remaining information in an efficient manner.

For instance, in the context of human speech, specialized techniques such as speech coding (or voice coding) are often used in lossy audio compression. These techniques are sometimes distinguished as a separate discipline from general audio compression. The compression of human speech is performed with even more specialized techniques to ensure that the essential elements of speech are preserved while non-essential components are removed.

### References

- [1] In lossy audio compression, methods of psychoacoustics are used to remove non-audible (or less audible) components of the audio signal.

Q: What heavily influenced nineteenth-century fictional depictions of John?
Gold: Ivanhoe
Answer: Nineteenth-century fictional depictions of John were heavily influenced by historical works, particularly Sir Walter Scott's historical romance, *Ivanhoe*. This work presented "an almost totally unfavourable picture" of the king and drew on Victorian histories of the period and Shakespeare's play. The influence of Scott's work extended to the late 19th-century children's writer Howard Pyle, who used it as a basis for his book *The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood*, which established John as the principal villain within the traditional Robin Hood narrative. These depictions were further perpetuated in various fictional books and films throughout the 20th century, often contrasting John with virtuous characters like King Richard or the more masculine Henry II.

### References

- [1] Nineteenth-century fictional depictions of John were heavily influenced by Sir Walter Scott's historical romance, *Ivanhoe*, which presented "an almost totally unfavourable picture" of the king; the work drew on Victorian histories of the period and on Shakespeare's play. Scott's work influenced the late 19th-century children's writer Howard Pyle's book *The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood*, which in turn established John as the principal villain within the traditional Robin Hood narrative. During the 20th century, John was normally depicted in fictional books and films alongside Robin Hood. Sam De Grasse's role as John in the black-and-white 1922 film version shows John committing numerous atrocities and acts of torture. Claude Rains played John in the 1938 colour version alongside Errol Flynn, starting a trend for films to depict John as an "effeminate ... arrogant and cowardly stay-at-home". The character of John acts either to highlight the virtues of King Richard, or contrasts with the Sheriff of Nottingham, who is usually the "swashbuckling villain" opposing Robin. An extreme version of this trend can be seen in the Disney cartoon version, for example, which depicts John, voiced by Peter Ustinov, as a "cowardly, thumbsucking lion". Popular works that depict John beyond the Robin Hood legends, such as James Goldman's play and later film, *The Lion in Winter*, set in 1183, commonly present him as an "effete weakling", in this instance contrasted with the more masculine Henry II, or as a tyrant, as in A. #2842
Q: Why were the controllers hard-wired to the console with no connectors?
Gold: cost reasons
Answer: The controllers were not hard-wired to the console with no connectors; instead, they used connectors designed to ensure a secure and reliable connection. For instance, the Game Cartridge Copper Connectors and Console Slot Nickel Connector Springs, which are components of the NES console, interacted in a way that facilitated the connection between the game cartridges and the console. However, these connectors faced issues due to wear and tear and corrosion over time. Frequent insertion and removal of cartridges caused the pins to wear out, and the ZIF (Zero Insertion Force) design proved more prone to interference by dirt and dust than an industry-standard card edge connector.

### References

- [1] When Nintendo released the NES in the US, the design styling was deliberately different from that of other game consoles. Nintendo wanted to distinguish its product from those of competitors and to avoid the generally poor reputation that game consoles had acquired following the video game crash of 1983. One result of this philosophy was to disguise the cartridge slot design as a front-loading zero insertion force (ZIF) cartridge socket, designed to resemble the front-loading mechanism of a VCR. The newly designed connector worked quite well when both the connector and the cartridges were clean and the pins on the connector were new. Unfortunately, the ZIF connector was not truly zero insertion force. When a user inserted the cartridge into the NES, the force of pressing the cartridge down and into place bent the contact pins slightly, as well as pressing the cartridge’s ROM board back into the cartridge itself. Frequent insertion and removal of cartridges caused the pins to wear out from repeated usage over the years and the ZIF design proved more prone to interference by dirt and dust than an industry-standard card edge connector. These design issues were not alleviated by Nintendo’s choice of materials; the console slot nickel connector springs would wear due to design and the game cartridge copper connectors were also prone to tarnishing. Many players would try to alleviate issues in the game caused by this corrosion by blowing into the cartridges, then reinserting them, which actually hurt the copper connectors by speeding up the tarnishing.
